hints: Look carefully at the y-axis in Fig. 6.2 at 1000 lux - is the value above or below zero, and what does a negative net uptake actually mean for gas exchange?
Think about what two opposite processes are happening at the same time in the leaf, one taking in CO2 and one releasing CO2.
Link the very low light intensity to the rate of the light-dependent reactions and decide which process is faster at 1000 lux.
walkthrough:
Read the Graph Value**
At 1000 lux find 1000 on the x-axis and go up to the curve. The y-value is below zero at about -1.6 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. Negative net uptake means overall CO2 is moving out of the leaf, not in.

Remember Net Uptake Is a Balance**
Living leaf cells always respire and release CO2, while photosynthesis in chloroplasts takes up CO2. What you measure is net: photosynthesis minus respiration. A negative value tells you respiration is winning.

Explain Why With Low Light**
At only 1000 lux there is very little light energy for the light-dependent reactions, so very little ATP and reduced NADP are made and very little CO2 is fixed in the Calvin cycle. Respiration continues, so more CO2 is released by respiration than is taken up by photosynthesis.

Final answer: At 1000 lux net CO2 uptake is negative, about -1.6 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$, so CO2 is released. Little photosynthesis occurs due to low light intensity, so rate of respiration is higher than rate of photosynthesis.

hints: Trace the curve from 2000 lux to 7000 lux - does the line go up, down or stay flat, and what does that say about CO2 uptake?
Pick two exact values from the graph with units to prove the trend, for example near 2000 lux and near 7000 lux.
Think about why more light lets the leaf fix more CO2 and what the term is for a factor that controls the rate in this rising section.
walkthrough:
Describe the Trend**
Between 2000 and 7000 lux the curve rises steeply. That means mean net CO2 uptake increases as light intensity increases.

Support With Numbers**
Always quote data in a graph question. At 2000 lux uptake is about -0.2 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$, close to the compensation point, and by 7000 lux it has risen to about 6.5 to 7.0 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. The units show you are comparing like with like.

Explain the Physiology**
More light means more energy absorbed by chlorophyll, faster light-dependent reactions, more ATP and reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle, so faster CO2 fixation. Because increasing light increases the rate, light is limiting the rate here.

Final answer: As light intensity increases from 2000 to 7000 lux, rate of CO2 uptake increases, e.g. from about -0.2 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ at 2000 lux to about 6.5 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ at 7000 lux. This is because rate of photosynthesis increases and light intensity is the limiting factor.

hints: If adding even more light above 10000 lux makes no difference to uptake, think about what else the Calvin cycle needs besides light products.
walkthrough:
Understand the Plateau**
Above 10000 lux the curve flattens at about 8.0 $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. Extra light energy cannot increase photosynthesis further, so light is in excess. Something else that the Calvin cycle depends on, such as CO2 concentration for fixation by Rubisco or temperature for enzyme activity, must now be holding the rate constant.
Final answer: Light intensity is no longer limiting; another factor such as CO2 concentration or temperature is now limiting.

hints: Insects are mainly made of protein and the enzyme is secreted into liquid outside the plant cells - what general class of hydrolytic enzyme breaks down protein?
walkthrough:
Match Substrate to Enzyme**
Insect bodies contain a lot of protein. To digest them into soluble small molecules the pitcher secretes enzymes into the fluid, so digestion is extracellular. A protease, also called proteinase or peptidase, hydrolyses peptide bonds in proteins to peptides and amino acids for absorption.
Final answer: Protease / proteinase / peptidase, an extracellular hydrolytic enzyme.

hints: Start with the nitrogen need - which large groups of molecules in plants contain nitrogen that could not be made without nitrates?
Recall the two main export products of the Calvin cycle that are used to build all other organic molecules - a 3-carbon acid and a 3-carbon sugar phosphate.
walkthrough:
Identify a Nitrogen-Requiring Product**
Nitrate provides nitrogen for amino groups and nitrogenous bases. Good examples are amino acids which are built into proteins, including enzymes and membrane carriers, or nucleotides which are built into DNA, RNA and ATP. All need nitrogen from nitrates.

Link to the Calvin Cycle Source**
The Calvin cycle fixes CO2 into glycerate-3-phosphate, GP, which is reduced to triose phosphate, TP. TP can be converted to amino acids when nitrogen is added, or GP and TP can feed pathways leading to nucleotides and other complex compounds. So naming GP or TP as the starting intermediate completes the link from photosynthesis to nitrogen metabolism.
Final answer: Compound that needs nitrogen: amino acids / proteins / nucleotides. Calvin cycle intermediate: glycerate-3-phosphate (GP) / triose phosphate (TP).
